title: When Rock Becomes Ore
question: What makes a rock worth mining?
hook: Plenty of rock contains metal, yet only some of it earns the name ore.
idea: Rock counts as ore only when the value of its minerals outweighs the cost of getting them out and processing them.

beats.prompt: A rock holds a little gold, but mining and refining it would cost more than the gold would sell for. Is it ore?

choices.label: Yes, because it contains gold
choices.feedback: Containing a valuable metal is not enough; ore also has to be worth mining.

choices.label: No, because it does not pay to mine
Yes, but only if the gold is pure
choices.feedback: Purity is not the test; ore is mixed with unwanted rock anyway. Cost against value decides.

choices.label: No, because ore never holds gold
choices.feedback: Native metals such as gold are among the minerals ores are mined for.

beats.explain: Ore must be economically viable to mine and process, so the value of its minerals has to beat the cost of extraction.

beats.prompt: Put these steps in order, from the mine to the waste pile.
items: Dig the rock out by mining
Free the ore from the gangue
beats.explain: Ore is mined, then processing first liberates it from the gangue and then concentrates the wanted mineral; the processed gangue is called tailings.

beats.prompt: Match each type of deposit to what it supplies.
beats.explain: Different geological processes build different deposits, and each type is a source of particular minerals.

beats.prompt: Sort each deposit type by how it formed.
beats.explain: Pegmatites and carbonatites are igneous rocks, while skarns and greisens are products of metamorphism.
